problem_motivation.content: Investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys are limited because applicable force fields are missing.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Computational investigations of structural, chemical, and deformation behavior in high-entropy alloys (HEAs), which possess notable mechanical strength, have been limited due to the absence of applicable force fields.

problem_motivation.content: The sparse literature on theoretical investigations and the high cost of experimental investigations create a need for computational methods.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: While research on HEAs is rapidly gaining interest, (1) the related literature on theoretical investigations is sparse and (2) experimental investigations are expensive and resource intensive.

problem_motivation.content: Classical MD simulations cannot provide accurate predictions for multi-element alloys due to a lack of robust intermolecular potentials.
problem_motivation.evidence_span: Classical MD simulations are unable to provide quantitatively accurate predictions of mechanical deformation for these multi-element alloys due to the lack of robust intermolecular potentials.

prior_approach.content: Earlier efforts relied on computationally expensive first-principles calculations which are limited by system size.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Thus, earlier efforts in the literature have primarily resorted to computationally-expensive and system-size-limiting first-principles calculations, which are restricted in scope for understanding the deformation dynamics of very large systems.

prior_approach.content: Previous studies reported the phase diagram of AlxCrCoFeNi alloys showing single-phase A1, single-phase A2, and two-phase regions based on Al content.
prior_approach.evidence_span: When the mole fraction of Al <0.3, a single-phase A1 is observed, and a single-phase A2 is found for Al >1.17, while a two-phase ( A1 + A2 ) for 0.3 ≤ Al ≤1.17 is reported [24] [26] .

prior_approach.content: Prior work used first-principles KKR-CPA methods to estimate formation enthalpies and predict phase stability.
prior_approach.evidence_span: Using the methods and approximations for accurate estimates of the formation enthalpy and relative energy of A1 and A2 phases [28] , the first-principles KKR-CPA results in Fig. 2 for Al of 0 < x < 2 mole fractions predict a similar global stability found in the experiment

prior_approach.content: Previous MD simulations of Al0.1CrCoFeNi HEA structure used Lennard-Jones potentials.
prior_approach.evidence_span: The MD simulations for investigating the structure of the Al 0.1 CrCoFeNi HEA [23] [56] have previously employed LJ potentials that cannot offer reliable predictions for such multi-component systems.

prior_limitation.content: First-principles calculations are restricted in scope and cannot handle very large systems needed for deformation dynamics.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: first-principles calculations, which are restricted in scope for understanding the deformation dynamics of very large systems.

prior_limitation.content: The previously used LJ potentials cannot offer reliable predictions for multi-component systems.
prior_limitation.evidence_span: LJ potentials that cannot offer reliable predictions for such multi-component systems

rejected_alternative.content: LJ potentials were avoided for Al-Cr and Co-Cr cross interactions because EAM/alloy parameters were unavailable.
rejected_alternative.evidence_span: Only the Al-Cr and Co-Cr cross interactions are modeled, using the Lennard-Jones (LJ) potential [23] [56] [57] , due to the lack of the available EAM/alloy parameters for these interactions.

causal_claim.content: An initial temperature rise from 300 K to 500 K caused an increase in Al-Al cluster size.
causal_claim.evidence_span: There is a marginal increase in the peak, g(r), of the Al-Al pairs in Fig. 7 while going from 300 to 500 K, which is attributed to an initial increase in the size of the Al-Al cluster size.

mechanism_principle.content: The decrease in Al-Al correlation above 500 K is caused by temperature-induced disorder in atomic rearrangement.
mechanism_principle.evidence_span: However, as a temperature rise induces disorder in the atomistic rearrangement, this correlation decreases above 500 K in the simulated HEA.

mechanism_principle.content: The difference in Al-Ni probability is attributed to the exclusion of the size effect (local site displacements) in the (k,T) calculations.

hypothesis_statement.content: The study proposes deriving intermolecular potential parameters using available ternary potentials to extend investigations.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: To extend investigations, we propose a set of intermolecular potential parameters for a quinary Al-Cr-Co-Fe-Ni alloy, using the available ternary Embedded Atom Method and Lennard-Jones potential in classical molecular-dynamics simulations.

hypothesis_statement.content: The authors hypothesize that high-strain compression will induce a clustering-to-ordering transition in the specific multi-element material.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: However, high-strain compression can induce a clustering-to-ordering transition in these multi-element materials.

hypothesis_statement.content: The study hypothesizes that the A1 Al0.1CrCoFeNi system will undergo clustering due to positive formation enthalpies.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: While the A1 phase is more stable than A2 for smaller x , the positive formation enthalpies of A1 and A2 phases imply that clustering is expected in the HEA.

hypothesis_statement.content: The study proposes that the A1 Al0.1CrCoFeNi alloy is unstable at the spinodal temperature, forcing clustering.
hypothesis_statement.evidence_span: The diverging Al-Ni pair of α αβ ( k = [000]) at the spinodal temperature (T sp ) indicates the absolute instability of the alloy that forces clustering in Al 0.1 CrCoFeNi

evidence_result.content: Calculated spinodal temperature matches experimental transition temperatures.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The calculated spinodal temperature, T sp = 840 K, shows good agreement with the experimentally-observed transition temperature of 813–823 K for Al x CrCoFeNi, 0 ≤ x ≤ 0.3 [24] .

evidence_result.content: MD simulations found a lattice parameter of 3.55 Å, agreeing with KKR-CPA and experimental values.
evidence_result.evidence_span: The MD simulations find 3.55 Å at 0 K, in reasonable agreement with KKR and experiment.

constraint.content: A cut-off radius of 10 Å was chosen to balance accuracy with computational time.
constraint.evidence_span: Thus, we employ a cut-off radius of r cut-off = 10 Å in all our MD simulations to obtain accurate results in a reasonable amount of computational time.

constraint.content: High strain rates of ~10^10 s^-1 were required due to length and time scale limitations in MD simulations, restricting the use of experimentally-realizable rates.
constraint.evidence_span: Higher strain rates, ~10 10 s −1 , are chosen to provide predictions within reasonable computational wall-clock times due to length and time scale limitations in MD simulations. This trend restricts the use of experimentally-realizable high strain rates, ~10 2 s −1 .
